posts:
A premier in polling freefall pivots his campaign against a foreign leader.

CBC: David Eby Campaign Analysis
Evidence: Defending BC, Scapegoating Trump, Securing power
#Aletheia #BCPoli #CDNpoli

Premier David Eby asserts an early snap election is essential to build a united provincial firewall against external trade threats from Donald Trump.

Stated Judgement: (+0.86, +0.75) — Greater Good

With his approval sliding to 31% over deficits and domestic policy reversals, Eby leverages foreign tariff rhetoric to sidestep provincial accountability and capture an early majority.

Resulting Judgement: (-0.88, -0.87) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Destruction. An opportunistic snap election uses an external villain to evade domestic policy scrutiny.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 16.2, Uncertainty z: 3)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- David Eby: FAIL (-0.88, -0.87) — Deflects domestic drops onto foreign threats.
- CBC Analysis: PASS (+0.72, +0.65) — Accurately notes poll dive and tactical pivot.
- Snap Election: FAIL (-0.82, -0.75) — Opportunistic early call harms norms.
Facing declining approval from 53% to 31% over domestic issues, BC Premier David Eby called a snap election, framing the race around standing up to Donald Trump.

The Bright Side:
US trade tariffs present real economic headwinds for British Columbia. However, using cross-border friction as a political smoke screen prevents an honest democratic debate on local governance.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The error swaps WHO for WHY. Instead of defending domestic fiscal and social policies, leadership manufactures an external adversary to consolidate electoral authority.

Social Physics Analysis:
Eby executes a classic Smart Selfish Maneuver. Plummeting approval is masked by projecting fear onto an external foil, manufacturing a false binary that demands uncritical loyalty while bypassing transparent review.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil. Democratic accountability is traded for political survival.

The Unavoidable Truth: Donald Trump is not running for office in British Columbia.

The Unavoidable Lie: Calling a snap election two years early is purely about protecting citizens from foreign tariffs.

Alethekanon:
Externalizing domestic political friction onto foreign leaders is a classic distraction technique. True democratic resilience begins with transparent stewardship of domestic policy, not manufactured emergencies.

Awwthekanon:
Citizens want leaders who listen to local struggles with housing and healthcare, not political maneuvers that use foreign headlines to distract from real community needs.

Brothekanon:
Your poll numbers tank so you call an early election and campaign against a guy in another country instead of your actual opponent. Classic political deflection, nobody's fooled.

Spirithekanon:
"Do not regard the faults of others, or what they have done or left undone; regard only what you yourself have done and left undone." Dhammapada 50 FAIL
Blaming external actors obscures personal duty and weakens systemic accountability.

Why David Eby is seemingly running for re-election against Donald Trump

If his first speeches are any indication, B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is running for re-election against one main opponent.

Actual Article Body:
If his first speeches are any indication, B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is running for re-election against one main opponent.

And it’s not B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson.

"There are big challenges out there for our province, challenges that are impacted by Trump's actions in positive and negative ways," said Eby at his day one campaign rally at the Canada-U.S. border, the unmistakable outline of the Peace Arch right behind him for the benefit of the cameras.

"I have a clear preference about which direction we should go: build up our province, strengthen our people, shoulder-to-shoulder across the country, standing up to Trump."

Overall, Eby said U.S. President Donald Trump’s name 18 times during Wednesday’s event. He said Trump’s name 19 times at his first public appearance to announce an election call. He said Doerkson’s name four times on Wednesday, and not once the day before.

For an indication as to why, look to both current events — but also the polls.

Why the B.C. NDP's David Eby seems to be running for re-election against Donald Trump

Since his re-election in 2024, Eby’s approval rating in the quarterly polls of all Canadian premiers done by the Angus Reid Institute has declined from a high of 53 per cent in March 2025 to 31 per cent in June of this year.

Whether it’s because of going back and forth on changes to the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, drug decriminalization, or the announcement of record deficits, the number of people inclined to voice their support for Eby in polls had been going down over the past 18 months.

And that was before any possible backlash of calling a snap election in the first place, which seems to have riled even mild mannered political scientists.

"A number of people would say, look, you may have the constitutional authority, but you shouldn’t do it," said Philippe Lagassé, a Carleton University professor and frequently cited expert on the Canadian constitutional system.

"It’s not very fair, it’s not very honourable, it’s not the right thing to do, it’s not very good for democracy. And I think there, I would agree," he said.

However, Eby’s high point of 53 per cent happened in the weeks after Trump kickstarted the current tensions with his threat of tariffs and 51st state rhetoric, which Eby responded to by removing American booze from government liquor stores.

Eby 'seems to be running against Trump more than anything' after calling snap election, pundit says

Perhaps that previous boost in popularity informed Eby’s rhetoric, perhaps not. But with a seeming lack of enthusiasm towards Eby, many political experts are saying it makes sense for the NDP leader to pivot to Trump.

"Eby benefits from this issue where he can now try to reposition the NDP as not a social democratic party, but a party that is pragmatic and following … Mark Carney's rhetoric, especially when it comes to trade and economic development," said Simon Fraser University political scientist Sanjay Jeram.

And that pivot, combined with all the uncertainty with the Conservative Party in the last year, may well work in Eby’s favour.

Liaison Strategies conducted a poll on Tuesday — the day Eby called the election — surveying 1,000 British Columbians with a margin of error of +/- 3.1 percentage points. And it showed the NDP with 41 per cent support, compared to the Conservatives with 36 per cent, the Greens at 12 per cent, and CentreBC and OneBC at four per cent each.

If that result held, it would likely give Eby the clear majority he argued is needed to build what he called a Trump firewall.

Which is why many see logic in the NDP’s approach, especially when one considers the state of the Conservative Party in the week leading up to the call.
